opinion.title: Opinion Announcement - June 24, 2019
opening: Justice Kagan has the opinion of the Court this morning, Case 18-302, Jansu v. Brunetti.

Kagan. The question in this case is whether a particular provision of the Federal trademark statute violates the First Amendment. A trademark, for anyone who doesn't know, is a brand name or a symbol or a saying or something of that kind that identifies a product. And if the trademark is registered with the U .S. Patent and Trademark Office, which I'll call the PTO for short, then the holder of the trademark gets certain legal benefits. But the trademark statute prohibits the PTO from registering certain kinds of trademarks. One of those prohibitions is what's at issue in this case. The statute says that the PTO can't register any immoral or scandalous trademarks. Today, we hold that provision to violate the First Amendment. The most fundamental principle of our free speech law is that the government can't penalize or disfavor or discriminate against expression based on the ideas and the viewpoints that it conveys. The ban on immoral or scandalous trademarks does just that. Trademarks are a kind of expression, and the statute's viewpoint discrimination is apparent from its very language. What does immoral mean? The dictionaries say, and you know this even without the dictionaries, that immoral means inconsistent with rectitude, purity, or good morals, violating principles of morality. And how about scandalous? Not really much different. According to the dictionary, something is scandalous when it gives offense to the conscience or moral feelings or when it's disgraceful or disreputable. So the immoral or scandalous bar allows trademark registration when a mark's message conforms with society's sense of decency and morality, but it prohibits registration of any mark expressing a contrary view when it goes against that societal sense of morality and rectitude. That's exactly the kind of discrimination against ideas that the First Amendment prohibits. Now, if that all sounds a little abstract, here are some examples that may make the point. The PTO rejected as immoral or scandalous trademarks for marijuana cola, and you can't spell health care without THC. Because, the PTO said, they glamorize drug use. But at the same time, the office allowed trademarks with sayings like, say no to drugs and dare to resist drugs.

The most fundamental principle of our free speech law is that the government can't penalize or disfavor or discriminate against expression based on the ideas and the viewpoints that it conveys. The ban on immoral or scandalous trademarks does just that. Trademarks are a kind of expression, and the statute's viewpoint discrimination is apparent from its very language. What does immoral mean? The dictionaries say, and you know this even without the dictionaries, that immoral means inconsistent with rectitude, purity, or good morals, violating principles of morality. And how about scandalous? Not really much different. According to the dictionary, something is scandalous when it gives offense to the conscience or moral feelings or when it's disgraceful or disreputable. So the immoral or scandalous bar allows trademark registration when a mark's message conforms with society's sense of decency and morality, but it prohibits registration of any mark expressing a contrary view when it goes against that societal sense of morality and rectitude. That's exactly the kind of discrimination against ideas that the First Amendment prohibits. Now, if that all sounds a little abstract, here are some examples that may make the point. The PTO rejected as immoral or scandalous trademarks for marijuana cola, and you can't spell health care without THC. Because, the PTO said, they glamorize drug use. But at the same time, the office allowed trademarks with sayings like, say no to drugs and dare to resist drugs. In other words, marks that express an anti-drug message. The office has similarly rejected immoral or scandalous views about, among other things, religion and terrorism, while approving marks expressing more accepted views on those same topics. The rejected marks express opinions that are offensive to many people in our society. But the First Amendment doesn't allow the government to discriminate against views just because many people, whether rightly or wrongly, view them as offensive. In an effort to save this statute, the government asks us to read it to mean something different from what it actually says. According to the government, we should read the statutes to cover only trademarks that are lewd, sexually explicit, or profane. But although we try to interpret statutes to avoid constitutional problems, we can't simply rewrite Congress's words. And the statute does not draw the line at lewd, sexually explicit, or profane marks. The statute may include those marks, but it also includes the universe of marks that convey immoral or scandalous ideas and viewpoints. And because that's so, the First Amendment requires that we strike the statute down. Justice Alito has filed a concurring opinion. Justice Sotomayor has filed an opinion concurring in part and dissenting in part, in which Justice Breyer joins.
